title: Jjimjilbang 2026: Your Ultimate First-Timer's Guide to Korean Saunas
description: Your first-timer's guide to Korean jjimjilbangs in 2026. Learn etiquette, what to bring, overnight stays, and recommended saunas for travelers in Seoul.

Your first-timer's guide to Korean jjimjilbangs in 2026. Learn etiquette, what to bring, overnight stays, and recommended saunas for travelers in Seoul.

Photo: 한건우 (Korea Tourism Org.) — 서울특별시 영등포구 양화동

Photo: 한건우 (Korea Tourism Org.) — 서울특별시 영등포구 양화동

What’s a jjimjilbang, anyway?

Okay, real talk: if you're hitting up Korea and haven't experienced a jjimjilbang, you're missing out. It’s not just a sauna, it's a whole vibe. Think of it as a Korean bathhouse meets spa meets a chill hangout spot. You can sweat it out in hot rooms, soak in pools, get a massage, grab a snack (hello, boiled eggs and sikhye!), and even crash overnight. Ngl, the first time can be a bit… intense. The communal nakedness is definitely a thing, but honestly, everyone’s just there to relax. It's a huge part of Korean culture, and once you get past the initial awkwardness, it's super therapeutic. Most jjimjilbangs are open 24/7, which is a lifesaver if you have a late flight or just want to pull an all-nighter.

The essentials: What to bring & what they give you

Good news: you don't need to lug your entire bathroom. When you pay the entrance fee (usually around ₩15,000-₩25,000, depending on the place and time), they'll give you a locker key, a bracelet, a small towel, and some cute little shorts and t-shirt uniform. It’s not high fashion, but it’s comfy for lounging. What *should* you bring? Definitely some flip-flops (though they usually have some too), toiletries like your toothbrush, toothpaste, and any skincare you're loyal to. If you’re super particular about towels, maybe bring your own microfiber one, but the ones they give are fine for basic drying. Oh, and a plastic bag for your wet clothes or dirty shoes.

Navigating the zones: Wet vs. Dry

This is where it gets specific. Jjimjilbangs are basically split into two main areas:

  • The wet zone (the baths): This is usually downstairs and where you get naked. Like, fully. There are usually several pools with different temperatures, plus showers everywhere. You gotta wash yourself *thoroughly* before getting into any of the pools. Seriously, soap up and rinse off completely. No street clothes allowed here.
  • The dry zone (the saunas & common areas): This is upstairs, where you wear the uniform. This is where you'll find the themed sauna rooms – think salt saunas, jade rooms, ice rooms, charcoal rooms. You can chill, nap, watch TV, play games, or hit up the restaurant here. This is the social part.

Most travelers stick to the dry zone for hanging out, but the real magic happens when you brave the wet zone. It’s worth it. Completely worth it.

Overnight stays: The ultimate budget hack?

Yep, you can sleep here. It’s kinda like a hostel, but way cheaper and you get unlimited sauna access. They usually have designated sleeping areas with mats and pillows on the floor. It’s not exactly luxury, but if you're on a tight budget or just need a place to crash for a few hours before an early flight, it's a solid option. Some places have family rooms or private sleeping pods if you’re not keen on sharing the main floor. Expect to pay a bit more for an overnight stay, maybe around ₩30,000-₩40,000. It’s definitely a unique experience, and honestly, waking up ready for a final soak? Priceless.

Which jjimjilbang for you? Traveler picks

For travelers, hitting up a well-known spot is usually easiest. They're more likely to have English signage and staff who are used to foreigners.

Siloam Spa (Seoul Station)

Exit 1, Seoul Subway Line 1, Seoul Station. Open 24 hours. This is a popular one right by Seoul Station, making it super convenient. It's pretty big with all the usual saunas and baths. Good for a first-timer who wants easy access and doesn't mind a slightly more commercial vibe.

Dragon Hill Spa (Yongsan) - TEMPORARILY CLOSED

Exit 1, Yongsan Station (Gyeongui-Jungang Line, ITX, KTX). Hours vary, check their site. This used to be the OG for many tourists, a massive complex with a pool, multiple saunas, and tons of amenities. It’s been closed for a while for redevelopment, so definitely check if it's reopened before you plan your trip! If it's back, it's a classic.

Itaewon Land

Exit 3, Itaewon Station (Seoul Subway Line 6). Open 24 hours. Located in Itaewon, this one's also convenient for travelers and has a good range of facilities. It's a bit more modern feeling than some of the older spots. Solid choice if you're staying in the Itaewon area.

FAQ

Q. Do I really have to be naked in front of strangers?
A. Yes, in the wet bath area. Everyone does it, and it's totally normal in Korea. You wear the provided uniform in the dry saunas and common areas.

Q. What if I’m uncomfortable with the nakedness?
A. Take it slow. Spend more time in the dry saunas and common areas first. Many people find they get used to it faster than they expect. Remember, the focus is relaxation, not judgment.

Q. Can I bring my own food and drinks?
A. Generally, no. Most jjimjilbangs have restaurants and snack bars where you can buy food and drinks. It's part of the experience!

Q. How much time should I budget for a visit?
A. Minimum 3-4 hours to really experience it. If you're staying overnight, obviously longer. Don't rush it!
